A little rocket science

FIELD NOTES
ENGINEERING FIELD NOTES

The numbers before
the engine.

The computer needs a consistent picture of the mission before it can decide when a burn should begin.

01 Where are we, and how fast?

A navigation state is two 3D vectors: position r in metres and velocity v in metres per second, measured in a named frame at a known time. A number without its frame or epoch is incomplete.

02 Why does orbital velocity matter?

An orbit is continuous free fall. Speed and direction determine the path. For the synthetic circular starting state, v = √(μ/r), where μ is the lunar gravity parameter and r is distance from the Moon’s centre. This checks the initial inputs; it does not fly the spacecraft.

03 Why calculate ignition time?

The same burn started at different positions reaches different places. Original P63 works backward from landing geometry and targets to calculate an absolute mission time for ignition. This demonstration stops at crew review before any ignition.

04 What is a guidance equation?

It is a mathematical relationship between the current state, a desired target and time. The flight software evaluates those relationships to plan a manoeuvre. Computing a plan is separate from applying physical thrust.

05 Why solve a polynomial?

Original ROOTPSRS searches for a root of A₀ + A₁x + A₂x² + A₃x³ = 0. The original guidance builds the coefficients from state and target data. Its root helps determine signed time-to-go; the browser never supplies the answer.

06 What if a landing site is missing?

A numerical routine cannot repair missing mission meaning. Scenario C omits RLS initialization. Follow the actual calculations to alarm 01406. The alarm is retained, not suppressed.

07 What changes at 16 kilometres?

A higher circular initial state has a different radius and speed. Original navigation and guidance recompute the solution. Compare scenarios A and B at their final events to see actual recorded differences rather than a browser estimate.

08 Original software or modern simulation?

The calculations and displayed events came from unchanged Luminary 099 running in the pinned AGC-compatible emulator. Mission inputs are synthetic. This page replays evidence and draws a static illustration; engine physics, powered descent and landing are not demonstrated.

09 Why align before navigating?

The computer needs to know how its inertial reference relates to space. Original P51 established reference-matrix readiness in this experiment using synthetic star sightings. That recorded readiness does not establish physical calibration of a real lunar module.

10 How will thrust and feedback work?

Thrust changes velocity through acceleration: a = F / m, where F is force in newtons and m is spacecraft mass in kilograms. A future external dynamics model must return validated sensor measurements to the AGC. The separate attitude lab already demonstrates bounded rotational feedback; translational burns are unavailable here.

Three seats. One mission.
